newsitem.title: USA: Bank of America extends healthcare to gay partners.
newsitem.headline: Bank of America extends healthcare to gay partners.

text.p: Bank of America, the third-largest U.S. bank, said Monday it would extend health benefits to the domestic partners of its gay or heterosexual U.S. employees starting next year.
Under its current policy, the bank, a unit of BankAmerica Corp, offers healthcare coverage to the spouses and dependent children of its 80,000 U.S. employees.
But starting Jan. 1, 1998, health coverage will be expanded to include employees' domestic partners, whether of the same or opposite sex, bank spokesman Dennis Wyss said.

Alternatively, an employee may choose to extend healthcare benefits to one dependent adult relative such as a parent, grandparent, brother or sister, Wyss said. Employees may enroll for the benefits, which include medical, dental and vision care, this fall.
A number of other large companies, many in the high-technology sector such as International Business Machines Corp and Hewlett-Packard Co, offer health benefits to same-sex domestic partners.

But Wyss said he believed San Francisco-based Bank of America was the only major U.S. bank to offer the extended health benefits. "It's part of our effort to create a workplace where members of our workforce are able to do their best work," he said.
News of the change was contained in Monday's edition of the bank's weekly employee newsletter, the "BankAmerican".

Late last year San Francisco's governing board of supervisors passed a local law requiring companies doing business with the city to provide equal benefits to spouses and employees' unmarried partners, whether gay or heterosexual.

Wyss said the ordinance was a factor in Bank of America's "decision-making process, but only one factor. We had been considering extending healthcare benefits for some time, well before the ordinance was introduced."
Bank of America already offers bereavement leave and family sickness leave to domestic partners, as well as to married couples, Wyss said.
Bank of America is a major employer in San Francisco, where it has more than 9,300 staff. It has contracts with the city, Wyss said without giving details. The new policy will apply nationwide.

Supervisor Leslie Katz, a co-author of the San Francisco ordinance, said she was "extremely pleased that Bank of America has taken a leadership role in the banking industry" by extending benefits to domestic partners.

"I believe Bank of America's action is an indication of the response we will see from other companies who want to contract with San Francisco. It is truly gratifying to see the impact our legislation is having," she added.

The bank newsletter said domestic partners applying for coverage "must be in a committed relationship that has existed for at least six months, and must be responsible for each other's welfare on a continuing basis." All other adults seeking coverage, except spouses, must be under 65 and must be the employee's dependent, the newspaper said.

Wyss said the bank could not estimate how much the new policy would cost because it did not know how many employees would take advantage of the added benefits. But based on the experience of other companies, "we believe that the cost will not be significant," he said.
